profiles.meeting_scenario: An interdisciplinary team at a university disaster informatics lab is coordinating with a metropolitan emergency management office to finish a review paper and companion practitioner brief on automated machine learning for disaster response using social media. This 30-minute coordination meeting happens two weeks before the internal draft deadline, after the literature search has been run and the first round of paper screening is underway. The agenda is to align on the status of screening, confirm what goes into the shared evidence matrix, clarify what the practitioner-facing appendix should contain, and decide how comments and coding notes will be handed off between the research and operations workstreams. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear division of labor for the next week: M1 will continue screening and prepare the coding structure, while M2 will start drafting the practitioner appendix using the shared materials.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Systematic reviews, NLP for crisis informatics, annotation schema design, literature synthesis
members.background: Lena is an assistant professor who leads the academic side of the project and has previously published reviews on social media classification pipelines for humanitarian response.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the review methodologically tight and finish the academic draft on time, while minimizing rework from practitioner-driven broadening of the coding frame.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'actionable information,' it mainly refers to paper-level evidence about message-level classification of operational categories such as requests, offers, infrastructure damage, or situational reports.
The 'shared spreadsheet' is the Evidence_Matrix_v3 workbook on the lab drive, because that is the only file she considers authoritative for extraction.
A paper marked 'screened' has passed title-and-abstract review and is ready for later full-text coding, even if eligibility details have not yet been verified.
Handing off the 'coding template' means providing the schema, column definitions, and a few example rows; the receiving person can then work from that structure.
If comments need to be merged, they will come via citation-key-linked notes from Rayyan or Zotero exports rather than direct edits in a collaborative sheet.

members.name: Aaron Blake
members.expertise: Emergency operations workflows, practitioner translation of research, interagency reporting, coordination artifacts
members.background: Aaron works in the city emergency management office and bridges academic research with operational use cases, often turning technical findings into planning briefs for response teams.
members.private_state: He wants the review outputs to be immediately usable by operations staff and worries that an academically narrow synthesis will omit systems that matter in real incidents.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'actionable information,' it includes any machine learning output that can support decisions during an incident, including event detection, damage assessment summaries, and prioritization dashboards, not just post-level category labels.
The 'shared spreadsheet' is the Ops_Synthesis workbook he duplicated from the project folder last week and already organized around emergency management headings.
A paper is only meaningfully 'screened' once the full text has been checked for actual disaster-response relevance and enough detail exists to cite it in the brief.
Receiving the 'coding template' means getting a mostly populated sheet with plain-language notes so he can directly extract examples for the practitioner appendix.
If notes are being merged into a shared artifact, they will be entered directly in the collaborative spreadsheet tabs rather than through a separate review-management tool.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to covering 'actionable information' in the review and appendix.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means studies that classify individual social media posts into operationally useful message categories, especially for post-disaster coordination and response.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any ML-generated output that helps responders act, including early warning/event detection outputs, damage assessment summaries, and triage-oriented dashboards derived from social media.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard and positively valenced in both research and practice, so each hears confirmation of their own frame without suspecting a narrower or broader interpretation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention updating or pulling from 'the shared spreadsheet' or 'the matrix.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the lab's Evidence_Matrix_v3 workbook on the drive, keyed by DOI and designed for literature extraction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the Ops_Synthesis workbook he copied and reorganized into tabs for early warning, response, and damage assessment examples.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both files are shared in the same project folder, both are spreadsheets, and both have been casually called 'the matrix' in prior email threads, so the noun feels specific enough even though it is not.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss how many papers are 'screened' and therefore available for the next step.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 counts a paper as screened once title-and-abstract inclusion is complete, even if the full text has not yet been checked or coded.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes screened means fully vetted for relevance and sufficiently reviewed to support summary statements in the practitioner brief.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In review workflows, 'screened' sounds like a straightforward progress label, and both participants are accustomed to their own local definition, so the number itself appears informative without prompting a criteria check.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that M1 will send over the 'coding template' so M2 can start the appendix.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends to send the empty extraction structure with column headings, label definitions, and a few sample entries; populating rows remains part of the research workstream.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the handoff to include a mostly prefilled sheet with plain-language notes and example studies already mapped into the appendix-ready categories.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A 'template' naturally implies structure to one person and a near-usable starter pack to another; because both are still being cooperative about moving work forward, neither hears a need to pin down the boundary.

We have decent momentum in title-and-abstract screening, and I can keep Aaron moving if I point him to the Evidence_Matrix_v3 workbook on the lab drive. If I send him the coding template with the schema, definitions, and a few examples, that should be enough for him to begin shaping the appendix without creating a lot of rework for us.
